title: Employed with a side of startup: how to run a startup on the side of a day job
summary: Jason Cohen explains how to start a company while employed without legal trouble. He covers choosing a business that fits your constraints, embracing slow growth, being open with your employer, and managing scarce time. Goal: build something solid enough to quit your day job.

principles.text: Turn side-gig constraints into competitive advantages instead of fighting them.
principles.quote: The right attitude is not only to work inside your constraints, but to turn them into competitive advantages!

principles.text: Pick a product where simplicity and few features is the selling point, since you lack time to build a bloated one.
principles.quote: "We do only one thing and we do it better than anyone" is a great marketing slogan. You don't have the time to make a Microsoft Excel knock-off, so don't!

principles.text: A bootstrapped side business should aim for slow, consistent growth; it maximizes odds of success and lets you change course early.
principles.quote: Slow growth maximizes your chance for success. Slow means your success is not dependent on some unlikely, massive event that's totally outside your control.

principles.text: The immediate goal is a business just solid enough to quit your day job, not millions.
principles.quote: your immediate goal isn't to make millions of dollars, it's to build a business just solid enough to quit your day job.

principles.text: Tell your employer about the side project, in writing, signed by someone with authority, to avoid lawsuits.
principles.quote: The best way to avoid a lawsuit is to prove that your employer knows you have a side project.

principles.text: Never use company laptops, software, or internet for the side business; assume everything is monitored and discoverable.
principles.quote: If your project is really on the side, you have no business doing business at work.
